title: Practice Passage 10: Can Boredom Be Beneficial?

passage.title: Can Boredom Be Beneficial?
passage.sub_title: Why escaping moments of mental inactivity with smartphones might be limiting our creative potential.
passage.content_html:
Paragraph A

[A1] For many years, boredom has generally been viewed as an unpleasant emotional state that people should avoid whenever possible. [A2] Modern technology makes escaping boredom easier than ever before, with smartphones, streaming services, and social media providing constant entertainment. [A3] As a result, many people now spend very little time without some form of external stimulation. [A4] However, psychologists have recently begun to question whether the complete elimination of boredom is actually desirable.

Paragraph B

[B1] According to several researchers, boredom is not simply the absence of activity. [B2] Instead, it is a psychological signal that encourages people to seek new goals, experiences, or solutions to existing problems. [B3] In this view, boredom functions in much the same way as hunger or thirst, reminding individuals that something requires attention. [B4] The writer believes this perspective provides a more balanced understanding of boredom than traditional assumptions.

Paragraph C

[C1] Some experiments have suggested that people occasionally produce more creative ideas after completing repetitive or uninteresting tasks. [C2] One explanation is that the mind begins to wander when it is not fully occupied. [C3] During this period, unrelated ideas may become connected in unexpected ways. [C4] Nevertheless, the writer accepts that creativity depends on many factors and should not be attributed solely to boredom.

Paragraph F

[F1] Technology companies are increasingly designing products to capture users' attention for as long as possible. [F2] Notifications, personalised recommendations, and endless scrolling all reduce opportunities for moments of mental inactivity. [F3] The writer is concerned that this constant stimulation may gradually reduce people's willingness to spend time thinking without distractions. [F4] However, this possibility remains the subject of ongoing research rather than established fact.

Paragraph G

[G1] Ultimately, boredom should neither be feared nor celebrated without careful consideration. [G2] Like many psychological experiences, its effects depend on the individual and the surrounding circumstances. [G3] The writer concludes that learning to tolerate occasional boredom may become an increasingly valuable skill in a world filled with constant digital stimulation. [G4] Rather than searching for entertainment every moment, people may sometimes benefit from allowing their minds the opportunity to slow down.

Paragraph D

[D1] Despite these possible benefits, boredom should not be romanticised. [D2] Long periods of boredom may reduce motivation and increase frustration, particularly when people feel unable to change their situation. [D3] The writer argues that the difference lies in duration and context. [D4] Brief periods of boredom may encourage reflection, whereas prolonged boredom often produces less positive outcomes.

Paragraph E

[E1] Schools provide an interesting example of this debate. [E2] Some educators believe every lesson should keep students continuously engaged through activities and technology. [E3] Others suggest that occasional quiet moments allow students to process information more deeply. [E4] The writer considers the second approach worthy of greater attention, although more evidence is still required.

question_data.text: The writer believes boredom has traditionally been viewed negatively.
question_data.common_mistake: Failing to connect 'generally viewed as an unpleasant state' with a negative historical view.

questions.explanation: Paragraph A states that for many years, boredom has generally been viewed as an unpleasant emotional state that people should avoid, showing agreement with the statement.
